metadata.file_name: 125. Huang & Keller (2025). Working with missing data in large‑scale assessments.pdf
metadata.title: Working with missing data in large-scale assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The tutorial’s applied example uses Belgian PISA 2018 student and school datasets and fits two-level random-intercept multilevel models. In the imputation and analysis workflow, the authors explicitly incorporate complex survey weights at both levels by specifying student weights (w_fstuwt) and school-level weights (w_schgrnrabwt) in the rblimp/Blimp imputation model and again in the WeMix model-fitting stage. The weights are treated as covariates/inputs to the imputation model (congenial imputation) and are also used in the substantive multilevel model with robust standard errors. Replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described in the excerpt, so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The applied tutorial example uses the Belgian PISA 2018 student and school datasets (merged, reduced dataset). The analytic focus is on predicting student mathematics abilities using 10 mathematics plausible values (pv1math–pv10math) and a multilevel structure with students nested in schools (cntschid). To demonstrate missing-data handling, the authors create an additional missingness scenario by selecting a variable with minimal missingness (escs, 2% missing) and then removing an additional 10% of escs values such that missingness is related to the first mathematics plausible value (missing at random). They then fit models on the original dataset (90% complete), the additional-missing dataset (82% complete), and the final multiply imputed datasets (200 multiply imputed datasets across 10 plausible values).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Belgium) — multilevel student (level 1) and school (level 2) model with plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effect estimates compared across three conditions: 90% complete data (results C), 82% complete data (results B), and multiply imputed datasets (results A) using 200 multiply imputed datasets (20 imputations per plausible value across 10 plausible values). No predictive accuracy metrics reported; differences assessed via coefficient similarity and random-effects ICCs.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (Belgium) the study leveraged Gender, ESCS, immigration status, student behavior hindering learning, and lack of teaching staff to model math achievement from plausible values, finding that results from the multiply imputed analysis (A) were closest to the 90% complete analysis (C), while the 82% complete analysis (B) showed larger discrepancies, especially for level-2 coefficients and the intercept. This indicates that multiple imputation in a multilevel, weighted plausible-values setting can reduce bias introduced by listwise deletion/complete-case reductions, supporting more transparent and less error-prone missing-data practice in LSA analyses.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Belgium) — multilevel random-effects model with plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects comparison across conditions: School intercept variance (τ00) 2675.176 (90% complete), 2099.088 (82% complete), 3282.989 (imputed); residual variance (σ²) 4397.184 (90% complete), 3895.583 (82% complete), 4150.606 (imputed). ICC values: 0.38 (90% complete), 0.35 (82% complete), 0.44 (imputed).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (Belgium) the study leveraged school and student predictors in a two-level random-intercept model and compared random-effects estimates across complete-case reductions versus multiply imputed datasets, finding that ICC was lower under the 82% complete condition (ICC=0.35) and higher under multiple imputation (ICC=0.44) relative to the 90% complete baseline (ICC=0.38). This indicates that missing-data handling can materially affect inferred between-school variability, implying that analysts should prefer multilevel multiple imputation over listwise deletion to avoid distorting conclusions about school-level differences.

data.outcome_summary: This article is a software tutorial focused on missing-data handling in large-scale assessments, using an applied example with Belgian PISA 2018 mathematics. The authors demonstrate how to impute missing predictors in a multilevel (students nested in schools) and weighted setting while accounting for plausible values (10 mathematics PVs). They compare three analytic conditions: the original dataset with 90% complete cases, a reduced dataset with 82% complete cases created by additional missingness in ESCS, and a multiply imputed dataset created via Blimp/rblimp with 20 imputations per plausible value (200 total imputed datasets). Rather than reporting predictive accuracy, they evaluate how fixed-effect estimates and random-effects components (including ICC) change across conditions, finding that multiply imputation yields results closest to the 90% complete baseline and alters between-school variance when compared with the 82% complete case. The tutorial emphasizes that listwise deletion can bias estimates when missingness is not MCAR and that congenial imputation should reflect the substantive model structure, including weights and plausible values.
